newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew braces for risky docking of supply ship.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew braces for risky docking of supply ship.

text.p: A supply ship is due to dock with Russia's Mir space station on Monday in a tricky operation crucial for the future of the troubled 11-year mission.
The two Russians and American aboard Mir spent Sunday resting and preparing for the docking, scheduled for 0959 Moscow time (0559 GMT).
The predecessor of the unmanned Progress craft launched on Saturday crashed into the station during docking on June 25 in the worst accident in the station's history.
Mir lost up to half its electric power in the collision and experts say this could hamper Monday's docking, which is supposed to happen automatically.

Progress is carrying oxygen, food and water as well as the tools needed to save the station and parcels from the families of the crew, who have had a nerve-wracking and uncomfortable time since the accident.
British-born American Michael Foale lost all his belongings in the crash and has asked NASA to send him a new toothbrush.
A NASA official said on Sunday the decision whether to send a replacement U.S. astronaut to Mir in September would rest on the assignment's likelihood of being safe and productive.

"There are two aspects to sending astronauts up to the MIR space station. First, is it safe? And secondly, is there a scientific and technical reason for doing that?" Daniel Goldin, NASA's administator, said on CNN's "Late Edition."
Navy Cmdr. Wendy Lawrence, 37, is slated to begin a four-month stay on Mir in September, replacing Foale, the fifth NASA astronaut to live and work on the station.

Foale and his Russian colleagues, flight commander Vasily Tsibliyev and engineer Alexander Lazutkin, talked to their families on Sunday and listened to music transmitted from mission control at Korolyov outside Moscow.
One of the operators making regular radio exchanges with the crew said they had played their favourite tunes but did not say what they were.

"The cosmonauts said they felt fine. Their blood pressure and temperature are normal. They are in a good mood," he said, adding that the crew would go to bed early. "They need to sleep well before tomorrow's hard day."
The three men will only get involved in the actual docking if something goes wrong but given the recent history of the station, they will need to be braced to act fast.
The crash during a manual docking procedure a fortnight ago sent air rushing out of the station from its damaged Spektr module. The crew would have suffocated if they had not sealed the hole quickly.

In doing so they had to sever the power supply from Spektr's undamaged solar panels, leaving the station with a dire shortage of electricity. Equipment to help them restore the supply is on board the new Progress.
In two pieces of good news, Mir's navigation system was repaired on Sunday in time for the docking and a problem with one of Progress's solar panels was overcome.
But even if Monday's docking goes without a hitch, the crew's problems are far from over.

Tsibliyev and Lazutkin will have to don spacesuits to fit a special airtight plate into the door of Spektr to feed 10 electric cables back into the main station. Foale is to sit out the repair inside the station's emergency escape ship.
Fellow cosmonauts at the Zvyozdny Gorodok (Star City) training centre near Moscow are testing the manoeuvres in a submerged mock-up of Mir.

But complications mean the actual repairs have already been put off by a week until July 17 or 18 and space officials are concerned that the leak this week of an unknown substance from Spektr may further increase the risks.
